lessons.title: Hedging & Academic Stance
lessons.tip: Strong professional and academic writing avoids unverified absolutes: use hedging («The data suggest that...», «tends to») to match the strength of your evidence.

exercises.title: Calibrating Claims with Evidence (Oxford CACE Reference)
exercises.body:
• Goal: distinguish sweeping assertions from cautious, evidence-calibrated English in reports and essays.
• Sweeping claim: «Remote work always destroys team cohesion.» (easily refuted by one counter-example).
• Calibrated stance: «Survey findings suggest that hybrid schedules may require clearer handover protocols.»

exercises.prompt: A pilot study of 40 commuters shows shorter wait times. Which sentence reports this accurately in a professional report?
options: Initial results indicate that the revised timetable may reduce average waiting times.
This study proves beyond doubt that no passenger will ever wait again.
Everybody obviously knows the new buses are perfect.
exercises.answer: Initial results indicate that the revised timetable may reduce average waiting times.
exercises.gradualHint: Match the certainty of your verb to a small 40-person pilot sample rather than universal proof.

optionExplanations.Initial results indicate that the revise: Spot on: «indicate» and «may reduce» accurately reflect preliminary evidence without overclaiming.
optionExplanations.This study proves beyond doubt that no p: Overgeneralises a 40-person pilot into an absolute guarantee («proves beyond doubt», «never»).
optionExplanations.Everybody obviously knows the new buses: Relies on informal emotional booster words («obviously», «perfect») instead of evidence.

exercises.sentence: Higher staff turnover ___ to increase training costs in the first quarter.
exercises.hint: Cautious generalisation verb (present simple, singular subject).
options: tends
proves
forces
exercises.gradualHint: Look for the verb followed by «to + infinitive» that expresses a frequent pattern rather than an iron law.

optionExplanations.tends: Correct: «tends to + infinitive» expresses a regular empirical pattern without claiming 100% inevitability.
optionExplanations.proves: «Proves to increase» changes meaning and claims absolute proof where a trend is described.
optionExplanations.forces: Grammatically requires a direct object («forces companies to increase»), so «forces to increase» is ungrammatical.

exercises.prompt: Los datos sugieren que hacen falta más pruebas.
exercises.answer: The data suggest that further testing is needed.
exercises.gradualHint: Start with «The data suggest that...» and use the formal collocation «further testing».

exercises.text: While the sample is small, the trend appears consistent
options: While the sample is small, the trend appears consistent
Because the sample is huge, the trend is finished
While the sample is small, the result is impossible
exercises.answer: While the sample is small, the trend appears consistent
exercises.gradualHint: Listen for the concession clause («While...») paired with cautious «appears consistent».

exercises.prompt: Second case: you need to acknowledge a limitation in your own proposal during a meeting. Which phrasing is strongest?
options: One limitation of this estimate is that winter demand has not yet been modelled.
Our estimate has zero flaws so nobody should question it.
Maybe everything in my spreadsheet is totally wrong, who knows.
exercises.answer: One limitation of this estimate is that winter demand has not yet been modelled.
exercises.gradualHint: Transparent professional English names the specific scope boundary calmly without self-sabotage or bluster.

optionExplanations.One limitation of this estimate is that: Excellent: naming the exact scope boundary builds credibility and invites constructive scrutiny.
optionExplanations.Our estimate has zero flaws so nobody sh: Dismissing scrutiny undermines trust as soon as a seasonal variable is raised.
optionExplanations.Maybe everything in my spreadsheet is to: Vague self-deprecation fails to identify which assumption actually needs checking.

exercises.prompt: Translate into formal English: «Sin embargo, los resultados varían según la región.»
alternatives: However, the results vary by region
However, results vary depending on the region
exercises.gradualHint: Open with «However,» and use «vary by region».

lessons.title: Argument Structure & Presentations
lessons.tip: Signpost each move in a presentation or essay: state your claim, anchor it in evidence, address counter-arguments, and state the practical implication.

exercises.title: Cohesive Paragraphing & Spoken Signposting
exercises.body:
• Goal: structure a clear argument (Topic Claim → Evidence → Counter-point → Conclusion) in written briefs and spoken presentations.
• Use signposting phrases («Turning now to...», «By contrast, ...») so listeners never have to guess how two ideas connect.
• Reference: practical academic/workplace English inspired by Oxford Language Centre CACE (distinct from literary criticism).

phrases.en: Turning now to the budget impact
To sum up our main recommendation

link.label: Council of Europe — CEFR B2/C1 Descriptors

exercises.prompt: In a presentation, you finish discussing staffing and want to move cleanly to safety metrics. Which signpost works best?
options: Turning now to safety metrics, let's examine last quarter's incident rate.
Anyway, random other thing, numbers!
As I already finished everything, goodbye—wait, safety.
exercises.answer: Turning now to safety metrics, let's examine last quarter's incident rate.
exercises.gradualHint: Choose the explicit transition marker that announces the new topic and tells the audience what to focus on.

optionExplanations.Turning now to safety metrics, let's exa: Clear and natural: «Turning now to...» signals a deliberate section shift for listeners.
optionExplanations.Anyway, random other thing, numbers!: Too informal and vague; listeners cannot tell how the slide relates to your argument.
optionExplanations.As I already finished everything, goodby: Signals a false ending and breaks the structure of the talk.

exercises.sentence: Upfront installation costs are higher; ___, long-term maintenance falls by 30%.
exercises.hint: Contrast connector between two clauses separated by a semicolon and comma.
options: however
despite
although
exercises.gradualHint: Check the punctuation: a semicolon before and a comma after («; ___,») requires a conjunctive adverb, not a preposition or subordinator.

optionExplanations.however: Correct: «; however,» links two independent clauses with contrast.
optionExplanations.despite: «Despite» is a preposition and must be followed by a noun phrase or -ing form, never a comma + full clause.
optionExplanations.although: «Although» introduces a subordinate clause without a following comma.

exercises.prompt: Para resumir, recomendamos una prueba piloto de tres meses.
exercises.answer: To sum up, we recommend a three-month pilot.
exercises.gradualHint: Hyphenated adjectives before a noun («a three-month pilot») stay singular in English.

exercises.text: Let me illustrate this point with a concrete example
options: Let me illustrate this point with a concrete example
Let me ignore this point without any example
Let me finish the report before the example
exercises.answer: Let me illustrate this point with a concrete example
exercises.gradualHint: Listen for the verb meaning to clarify an argument through a specific case.

exercises.prompt: Second case: during Q&A, someone asks for a figure you don't have in front of you. How do you respond professionally?
options: I don't have the exact breakdown to hand, so I'll verify it after the session and send it over today.
I'll invent 42% right now so I look confident.
That question is forbidden.
exercises.answer: I don't have the exact breakdown to hand, so I'll verify it after the session and send it over today.
exercises.gradualHint: Professional credibility comes from stating what you know, declining to guess, and committing to a concrete follow-up.

optionExplanations.I don't have the exact breakdown to hand: Spot on: «to hand» is idiomatic British English, and promising verified follow-up protects accuracy.
optionExplanations.I'll invent 42% right now so I look conf: Guessing numbers in a meeting risks false decisions and damages trust.
Hostile and unprofessional in workplace or academic Q&A.

exercises.answer: Turning now to the second point
alternatives: Moving on to the second point
exercises.gradualHint: Use the presentation signpost from the opening card: «Turning now to...».
